title: Rome falls (410)
hookLine: the city is sacked, and Augustine writes City of God: two cities, two loves

lines: THE OLD GODS, OR THE NEW ONE?
A BISHOP PICKS UP HIS PEN.
cards: The news crosses the sea, and it's hard to believe. Rome has been sacked. An army of Goths has broken into the city and plundered it.

People who fled are arriving. And some say out loud what they're thinking: this happened because Rome turned from its old gods to the Christian one. Across the water in Africa, Augustine is now a bishop.
He hears the charge, picks up his pen to answer it, and the answer grows into a very long book.

teach.b: The book is The City of God. Augustine starts with the charge itself.

During the sack, he points out, the invaders spared people who fled into the churches of the apostles, and some of those spared are now the ones blaming Christ. Then he goes much further than a reply.
There are two cities mixed together in this world, he says.

teach.h: NO EMPIRE IS THE CITY OF GOD.
teach.b: The Psalms sing of one, in the King James words: "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God." Beside it Augustine sets the earthly city. Then comes the line that holds the whole book together.
Two loves have made two cities. Love of self, reaching even to contempt of God, made the earthly city. Love of God, reaching even to contempt of self, made the heavenly one.
That changes the question. For Augustine, Rome was never the city of God, not even a Christian Rome. No empire is.
The two cities run through every street and every church, tangled together until the end. So when Rome falls, he tells his readers, they may grieve, but their hope was not built on its walls.
The letter to the Hebrews had said it: "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come." That's no excuse to stop caring.
The heavenly city, Augustine says, while on pilgrimage here, makes use of the earthly city's peace and seeks it, since its people share that life too.
But every city, party and institution faces the same question: what does it love? And the question runs through each person, too.

how: Augustine's City of God is read and taught by Christians of different churches, especially when they think about faith and public life; his image of two cities and two loves is often cited in that conversation.

games.q: you're a bishop. people who fled Rome are arriving, and some say the city fell because it abandoned its old gods. what do you do?
o: say nothing: the talk will pass.
answer the charge, then write about two cities and two loves.
say God punished Rome, and leave it there.
games.why: Augustine answered, and kept going. his reply became The City of God: no empire is God's city; two loves build two cities.

practice: Think of the places your days go into: your work, your home, a group you belong to, the screen in your pocket.

Pick one, and ask Augustine's question of it quietly: what does it love, and what am I adding to it, love that curls inward or love that turns outward? Don't grade yourself; just look, and if you pray, offer that place to God.
